overview: Eoraptor lunensis ("dawn thief of the valley of the moon") is one of the earliest dinosaurs, from the Ischigualasto Formation of Argentina (~231 Ma). At 1.7 metres long and about 10 kg, it was a small, generalist predator-omnivore with a mixed dentition — leaf-shaped teeth for plant material and recurved teeth for flesh. Its exact position in the dinosaur tree has shifted repeatedly: originally considered a basal theropod, it is now placed as a basal sauropodomorph.

The discovery of Eoraptor in 1991 by Paul Sereno's team, alongside Herrerasaurus and the ornithischian Pisanosaurus, confirmed that the major dinosaur lineages diverged rapidly from a common ancestor in the Late Triassic. Its mixed dentition — an omnivorous toolkit — may represent the ancestral dinosaur condition before the dietary specialisations of later groups evolved.

articles.title: Discovery and shifting classification
articles.body: Paul Sereno and colleagues described Eoraptor lunensis in 1993. Initially classified as a basal theropod, cladistic reanalysis from 2011 onward consistently places it as a basal sauropodomorph. The mixed dentition — leaf-shaped posteriorly, recurved anteriorly — is unusual and may reflect an omnivorous generalist diet ancestral to the herbivorous sauropodomorphs that followed.

articles.title: Anatomy
articles.body: Eoraptor had a small skull with large eyes, a lightly built skeleton and hindlimbs suited for bipedal running. Unlike Herrerasaurus, it lacks the specialised intramandibular joint and is considerably smaller. Five fingers are retained on the hand, with the fourth and fifth being vestigial — a condition more primitive than Herrerasaurus.

articles.title: Dawn of the dinosaurs
articles.body: The Ischigualasto Formation at 231 Ma captures one of the earliest moments of dinosaur diversification. All three major dinosaur groups — Saurischia, Ornithischia and what may be their earliest relatives — are represented in the same beds. Eoraptor's small size and generalist diet are consistent with an ancestral ecological role before the dietary and size diversification that would characterise later dinosaur evolution.

animalParagraphs: Eoraptor was a small, lightly built biped only about a metre long and perhaps ten kilograms in weight. It lived in the Ischigualasto valley about 230 million years ago alongside Herrerasaurus, Eodromaeus and a fauna dominated by rhynchosaurs, cynodonts and pseudosuchian archosaurs.

Its skull was low and slender with a long snout. The teeth are the puzzle: the front of the jaw carries leaf-shaped teeth like those of plant-eating sauropodomorphs, while further back they become recurved and serrated like a predator's. This mixture is often read as omnivory, but tooth shape alone cannot settle what it ate.

Named in 1993 as one of the most primitive dinosaurs known, Eoraptor was first treated as a basal theropod. The full description of the skeleton in 2013 moved it to the base of Sauropodomorpha, the lineage leading to the giant sauropods, and most analyses since have followed, though its position remains sensitive to dataset choice.
animalHighlights: A nearly complete skull and skeleton makes it one of the best-preserved Triassic dinosaurs of its size.
Leaf-shaped front teeth and recurved rear teeth hint at a mixed diet that cannot be confirmed.
Reclassified from earliest theropod to earliest sauropodomorph as analyses improved.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Heterodont teeth suggest a varied diet, but no gut contents, wear studies or coprolites tie the animal to specific food.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Long hindlimbs and short arms with grasping hands in the holotype show habitual two-legged movement.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: The near-complete skeleton gives a reliable length; mass is estimated from limb bone dimensions and the animal's growth stage is not fully resolved.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Proportions come from the articulated holotype; skin, colour and any filamentous covering are not preserved.

presentation.classificationSummary: Eoraptor is an early saurischian whose exact position is contested. The 2013 monograph and most later analyses place it at the base of Sauropodomorpha, but some studies recover it as a basal theropod or as a saurischian outside both groups, so the catalogue marks the sauropodomorph placement with a query.

questions.title: What did it eat?
questions.copy: The teeth combine plant-eater and predator shapes. Omnivory is the usual reading, but it remains an inference from tooth form rather than direct evidence.

questions.title: Sauropodomorph or theropod?
questions.copy: Its placement shifts with the characters and taxa included in each analysis. The current majority view favours the sauropodomorph stem.

questions.title: Was the holotype fully grown?
questions.copy: Bone surface texture and skeletal fusion suggest the animal was not a juvenile, but adult size and growth pattern are not firmly established.

review.ageReviewNote: Radiometric dates constrain the fossil-bearing Ischigualasto interval near 231-229 Ma.

specimens.name: Holotype
specimens.institution: Museo de Ciencias Naturales, Universidad Nacional de San Juan
specimens.note: Articulated, nearly complete skeleton with skull found in 1991 in the Valle de la Luna.

panel.headline: A nearly complete articulated skeleton, plus a few partial referred specimens.
panel.standfirst: Eoraptor rests on the holotype PVSJ 512, an articulated skeleton with skull that preserves the great majority of the animal. Additional partial specimens from the same formation add little that the holotype does not already show.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every skeletal region is preserved in the articulated holotype, including a complete skull, hands and feet, with parts duplicated in referred specimens.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: A complete skull with lower jaws and full dentition, the entire vertebral column with ribs and chevrons, both girdles, forelimbs with hands, and hindlimbs with feet, largely in articulation.
knownRemains.note: Some elements are crushed or damaged and the tail tip is incomplete; referred specimens are less complete than the holotype.

media.caption: A skeletal diagram of Eoraptor lunensis showing preserved elements in white and unknown regions in grey; almost the whole skeleton is documented.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: A complete skull with braincase, lower jaws and the full heterodont tooth row.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Cervical, dorsal, sacral and most caudal vertebrae, with ribs, gastralia and chevrons.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Scapulocoracoids, complete pelvis, both forelimbs with five-fingered hands, and both hindlimbs with feet.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: None. No skin, integument, gut contents or eggs are known.
